questions.stem: The net cost price of exactly 20 articles is strictly the same as the final selling price of exactly 15 articles. What is the precise profit percentage?
questions.explanation: Let CP of 1 article be x. CP of 20 = 20x. SP of 15 = 20x, so SP of 1 = 20x/15 = 4x/3. Profit on 1 article = (4x/3) - x = x/3. Profit % = (Profit / CP) * 100 = (x/3 / x) * 100 = 100/3 % = 33.33%.

questions.stem: If a vintage radio is purchased for exactly Rs. 490 and formally sold for exactly Rs. 465.50, reliably find the exact loss percentage.

A retail shopkeeper sadly sells an imported article at a net loss of exactly 8%. If he had successfully sold it for precisely Rs. 36 more, he would have strictly gained exactly 4%. Find the absolute cost price of the article.
questions.explanation: Let the CP be x. First SP = x - 0.08x = 0.92x. Second SP = x + 0.04x = 1.04x. Difference between the two selling prices is 1.04x - 0.92x = 0.12x. We are given 0.12x = 36. So x = 36 / 0.12 = 300. Thus, CP is Rs. 300.

questions.stem: A smart trader thoroughly mixes exactly 26 kg of fine rice at Rs. 20 per kg with entirely 30 kg of rice of another variety at Rs. 36 per kg and safely sells the final mixture at Rs. 30 per kg. His exact profit percent is:
questions.explanation: Total Cost Price (CP) = (26 * 20) + (30 * 36) = 520 + 1080 = 1600. Total quantity = 26 + 30 = 56 kg. Total Selling Price (SP) = 56 * 30 = 1680. Profit = 1680 - 1600 = 80. Profit % = (Profit / Total CP) * 100 = (80 / 1600) * 100 = 5%.

questions.stem: By firmly selling a manufactured article for exactly Rs. 100, a man comfortably gains exactly Rs. 15. Then, his precise strict gain percentage is:

options.option_text: 15% (alternative interpretation)
20% (alternative interpretation)

questions.stem: A person completely sold a fine horse at a healthy gain of exactly 15%. Had he aggressively bought it for exactly 25% less and strictly sold it for exactly Rs. 600 less, he would have remarkably made a strong profit of precisely 32%. The absolute initial cost price of the horse was:
questions.explanation: Let original CP = 100x. Original SP = 115x. New CP = 100x - 25% = 75x. New SP = 115x - 600. The profit on New CP is 32%. New SP = New CP + (32% of New CP) = 75x + 0.32(75x) = 75x + 24x = 99x. We equate the two forms of New SP: 115x - 600 = 99x => 16x = 600 => x = 600/16 = 37.5. Original CP = 100x = 3750.

questions.stem: A heavily dishonest local dealer strongly professes to sell his retail goods exactly at cost price, but he silently uses a false weight of 960 grams for a standard kg weight. Accurately find his exact true gain percent.

options.option_text: 5% (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Error = 1000g - 960g = 40g. The dealer charges the customer for 1000g but only delivers 960g. His real cost is the 960g he delivered. Gain % = (Error / False Weight) * 100 = (40 / 960) * 100 = (1 / 24) * 100 = 100 / 24 = 25 / 6 = 4 1/6 %.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then offers a 15% discount on the marked price. What is his net profit percentage?

options.option_text: Profit of 17% over the original cost price
Profit of 19% over the original cost price
Profit of 21% over the original cost price
Profit of 25% over the original cost price

questions.explanation: Let CP = 100. MP = 140. SP = 140 × 0.85 = 119. Profit = 19%. Option C (21%) is the most tempting mistake — candidates incorrectly add the mark-up and subtract the discount (40 − 15 − 4 = 21) without accounting for the multiplicative effect of the discount on the inflated marked price.

questions.stem: A vendor sells 12 pens for the same total price as it costs him to buy 15 pens. What is his profit percentage?

options.option_text: Profit of 20% on the total purchase cost
Profit of 25% on the total purchase cost
Profit of 15% on the total purchase cost
Profit of 30% on the total purchase cost

questions.explanation: SP of 12 pens = CP of 15 pens. Profit on 12 pens = CP of (15 − 12) = CP of 3 pens. Profit % = (3/12) × 100 = 25%. Option A (20%) is wrong because candidates mistakenly compute 3/15 × 100 = 20%, dividing by the selling quantity 15 instead of the buying quantity 12.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper allows a discount of 10% on the marked price and still earns a profit of 17% on the cost price. By what percentage has he marked the article above its cost price?

options.option_text: Marked up by 25% over the cost price
Marked up by 27% over the cost price
Marked up by 30% over the cost price
Marked up by 35% over the cost price

questions.explanation: Let CP = 100. SP = 117. Since SP = 0.9 × MP, we get MP = 117/0.9 = 130. Mark-up = 30%. Option B (27%) is a common error — candidates compute the discount as a fraction of CP instead of MP, or misread the relationship between 10% discount and 17% profit as (17 + 10) = 27%.

questions.stem: A trader marks his goods 25% above cost price and then offers successive discounts of 10% and 4% to the buyer. What is his net profit or loss percentage on the cost price?

options.option_text: Net profit of 10% on the original cost price
Net profit of 8% on the original cost price
Net loss of 2% on the original cost price
Net profit of 6% on the original cost price

questions.explanation: CP = 100, MP = 125. After 10% discount: 125 × 0.90 = 112.5. After 4% discount: 112.5 × 0.96 = 108. Net profit = 8%. Option A (10%) is wrong because candidates add the successive discounts as 10 + 4 = 14% on MP giving 125 × 0.86 = 107.5 (≈7.5% profit), or mistakenly assume the discounts partially offset each other to land on 10%.

questions.stem: A seller marks an article 35% above its cost price. To earn exactly 8% profit on the cost price, what percentage discount must he offer on the marked price?

options.option_text: Discount of 15% on the marked price
Discount of 18% on the marked price
Discount of 20% on the marked price
Discount of 25% on the marked price

questions.explanation: CP = 100, MP = 135, required SP = 108. Discount = (135 − 108)/135 × 100 = 27/135 × 100 = 20%. Option B (18%) is a frequent error — candidates compute (135 − 108)/100 × 100 = 27%, then confuse numerator/denominator or subtract 35 − 8 = 27 and halve it, arriving at ≈18%.

questions.stem: A trader buys 80 oranges for Rs. 240. He discards 20 that are unfit for sale. He wants to earn exactly 20% profit on his total purchase cost. At what price (in Rs.) must he sell each remaining orange?

options.option_text: Rs. 4.50 per sellable orange
Rs. 4.80 per sellable orange
Rs. 5.00 per sellable orange
Rs. 5.40 per sellable orange

questions.explanation: Total CP = Rs. 240. Required SP = 240 × 1.20 = Rs. 288. Sellable oranges = 80 − 20 = 60. SP per orange = 288/60 = Rs. 4.80. Option C (Rs. 5.00) is wrong when candidates compute 20% profit on 60 oranges only (cost attributed as 60/80 × 240 = 180; SP = 216; per unit = 3.60 — another common wrong path) or round 288/60 up to 5. Option A arises from computing 240/60 × 1.125.

questions.stem: A manufacturer sells goods to a wholesaler at 20% profit; the wholesaler sells to a retailer at 15% profit; the retailer sells to a customer at 25% profit. If the customer pays Rs. 2,070, what is the manufacturer's cost price?

options.option_text: Rs. 1,000 as manufacturer's cost price
Rs. 1,200 as manufacturer's cost price
Rs. 1,400 as manufacturer's cost price
Rs. 1,500 as manufacturer's cost price

questions.explanation: Let manufacturer's CP = x. Chain: x × 1.20 × 1.15 × 1.25 = 2070. Compute: 1.20 × 1.15 = 1.38; 1.38 × 1.25 = 1.725. So x = 2070/1.725 = 1200. Option C (Rs. 1,400) is the most tempting error — candidates add 20 + 15 + 25 = 60% and compute 2070/1.60 ≈ 1294, then round to 1,400, ignoring the compounding nature of successive markups through the supply chain.
